abstract: Ensuring ecosystems are stable has become a priority given humanity's dependence on the services those ecosystems provide. There has consequently been significant research effort demonstrating that ecosystem stability is driven by 'response diversity', whereby different species respond uniquely to the environmental conditions and 'insure' the ecosystem against collapse. However, response diversity theory has only been applied at the ecosystem/community level, when the response diversity of individual animals' behaviour or traits is also theoretically linked to population-level stability. Therefore, we may be overlooking a viable indicator of extinction risk. Using long-term behavioral and energetic expenditure data from two seabird species breeding in the North Atlantic (Atlantic puffin Fratercula arctica and black-legged kittiwake Rissa tridactyla), we demonstrate that the response diversity in foraging effort of individual birds correlates with the stability of their colony's population size, while energetic expenditure does not. Further, the diversity of bird responses increases when environmental conditions (here represented by sea surface temperature) are outside of the colony's norm. Our work shows that response diversity provides a new perspective on the role of individual behavioral differences in creating stable populations, offering insights to better manage vulnerable groups.
